Selected place or object

Narthex

The narthex is the church’s entrance or vestibule. The OCA describes several rites held there and differences among architectural traditions.

[3] Answer, paragraphs on the vestibule/narthex

The Vestibule (Pritvór), or inner porch, was appointed, in early times, for the Catechumens, or learners, and for penitents. Here they listened to exhortations and instruction, and here they prayed. The rubric decrees that the Office for the Reception of Converts shall be performed in this Vestibule. Several of the penitential Offices, also, are appointed to be said here, such as the Litiyá (a litany of fervent supplication, with oft-repeated "Lord, have mercy" in response) at Vespers.

[1] The Symbolism of the Church, p. xxxii, Vestibule

Edition and layout notes

Orthodox church plans and decoration vary by architectural tradition. This map illustrates one Russian arrangement, not every Orthodox parish.

[3] Answer, opening paragraph and final paragraph

Fitzgerald’s Greek-tradition description places the patronal icon on the other side of the screen. The selected diagram follows Hapgood’s Russian arrangement; patron placement varies.

[4] Iconostasion, paragraph on icon positions · [1] The Symbolism of the Church, p. xxxi, customary arrangement, On the right of the Holy Door

Fitzgerald also describes a bishop’s throne on the right side of the Greek-tradition nave. This differs from the high-place seat behind the Holy Table illustrated here.

[4] Sacred Space, paragraph on the nave · [1] The Symbolism of the Church, p. xxix, Behind the Altar is the High Place

The font’s floor position in this drawing is illustrative. The cited Hapgood passage identifies its baptismal use, rather than prescribing the position shown in this diagram.

[1] Holy Baptism, immersion rubric; illustration placement note

The choir positions in the diagram illustrate Hapgood’s two choir places. The map’s dimensions, object spacing, and drawn routes are editorial geometry rather than a measured plan for every parish.

[1] The Symbolism of the Church, p. xxvii, two choir places

If there is to be a sermon, the Priest may preach it immediately after the reading of the Gospel, or at the end of the Liturgy.

The historical edition itself gives alternate sermon placement. The sequence does not claim one compulsory placement for every parish.

[2] Appendix B, IV, The Liturgy, note 14

Source context

The physical layout and principal liturgical excerpts follow Hapgood’s 1906 Russian-tradition service book. This is an observational study guide. Its clergy rubrics, seasonal alternatives, and historical explanations remain attributed to that edition. The visitor cards reproduce separately identified parish guidance; they are not a newly assembled universal prayer or worship rule.

Necessary concise source-bound summary; the cited modern prose is not reproduced in full, or an OCR-damaged historical passage needs a readable factual description.
